title: Define production and understand the basic activities of production / conversion in the agri-business environment

lessons.title: What production means on a farm
lessons.html:
What is production?

Production means making something that people need and will pay for. On a farm we produce food, fibre and other goods. A maize farmer produces grain. A dairy farmer produces milk. A sheep farmer produces wool and meat.

Every farm takes things in, works with them, and sends something out. We call this the production process.

Inputs

Inputs are the things we put into production. Some examples:

  • Seed, seedlings and young animals
  • Fertiliser, feed, water and medicine
  • Diesel, tools, tractors and a bakkie
  • Land, such as fields, camps and veld
  • People: your work and the work of your team
  • Money to pay for all of this

The process

The process is the work we do with the inputs. We plough and plant. We water, weed and spray. We feed, dip and check the animals. We milk the cows. Each job adds value, because it helps the crop or animal grow.

Outputs

Outputs are what comes out at the end. A bag of maize, a crate of tomatoes, a litre of milk, a weaner calf or a bale of wool are all outputs. Some outputs are waste, like manure or crop leftovers. Good farmers use waste again, for example manure as fertiliser.

A simple example

Think of a vegetable garden on the farm. The inputs are cabbage seedlings, compost, water and two workers. The process is planting, watering, weeding and harvesting. The output is heads of cabbage that are sold at the local market for rand. If the money from the cabbages is more than the cost of the inputs, the garden makes a profit.

When you understand inputs, process and outputs, you understand why your job matters. If one step is done badly, the output is smaller or poorer, and the farm earns less.

lessons.title: Conversion: adding value to farm products
lessons.html:
What is conversion?

Conversion means changing a raw farm product into a different product. The new product is usually worth more money. This is also called processing or adding value.

Examples of conversion

Raw productConverted product
MilkCheese, maas, yoghurt
Maize grainMaize meal
TomatoesTomato sauce or chutney
CattleMeat and hides
WoolYarn and cloth
GrassHay bales or silage

Animals also convert. A cow converts grass from the veld into milk and meat. Chickens convert feed into eggs. This is why we must feed animals well: poor feed means poor output.

The basic activities

Most production and conversion on a farm follows the same steps:

  1. Plan what to produce and how much.
  2. Get inputs ready, such as seed, feed and tools.
  3. Grow or raise the crop or animals.
  4. Harvest or collect the product.
  5. Process or convert it, if the farm does this.
  6. Store and pack it safely and cleanly.
  7. Sell and deliver it to the buyer.

Your part in the chain

Every worker is part of this chain. The person who packs tomatoes is as important as the person who plants them. If tomatoes are bruised in the crate, the buyer pays less. If milk is not kept cold, it goes sour and cannot be made into cheese.

Quality and safety

Converted food is eaten by people, so it must be clean and safe. Wash your hands, keep work areas clean and follow the farm rules for hygiene. Report any product that looks spoiled to your supervisor.

Key points

  • Production turns inputs into outputs through a process.
  • Inputs include land, seed, feed, water, tools, money and people.
  • Conversion changes a raw product into a product worth more.
  • Every step in the chain affects the quality and price of the product.
  • Clean, careful work protects the farm's income.
